raw_segments.text: And when she was gone, Socrates, sitting up on the couch, bent and rubbed his leg, saying
as he was rubbing, how singular is the thing called pleasure, and how curiously related
to pain, which might be thought to be the opposite of it.
For they are never present to a man at the same instant, and yet he who pursues either
is generally compelled to take the other.
Their bodies are too, but they are joined by a single head.
And I cannot help thinking that if Aesop had remembered them, he would have made a fable
about God trying to reconcile their strife, and how, when he could not, he fastened their
And this is the reason why when one comes the other follows, as I know by my own experience
now, when after the pain in my leg which was caused by the chain pleasure appears to succeed.
